conventional_description: Interstitial Lung Disease is an umbrella term for a group of disorders that cause progressive scarring (fibrosis) of the lung tissue. This scarring makes the lungs stiff and reduces their ability to transfer oxygen into the bloodstream, leading to persistent dry cough and gradually worsening shortness of breath. Diagnosis typically involves high-resolution CT scans, pulmonary function tests, and sometimes a lung biopsy to determine the specific type and extent of damage.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management aims to slow disease progression and relieve symptoms. Anti-fibrotic medications like pirfenidone and nintedanib can slow lung function decline in some patients. Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants are used when inflammation is prominent. Supportive care includes supplemental oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, and in advanced cases, lung transplantation. Vaccinations and prompt treatment of respiratory infections are also emphasized.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, Interstitial Lung Disease is viewed through the lens of Fei Wei - a withering and weakening of the lung tissue itself. The Lungs are responsible for descending Qi and distributing fluids throughout the body. When they become chronically undernourished or obstructed, the delicate lung structures lose their suppleness and can no longer perform these functions properly. This explains the hallmark dry cough and breathlessness, but also why the condition can manifest so differently from person to person.
The root of the problem often lies not just in the Lungs but in the Spleen, Kidneys, and Liver. The Spleen produces the Qi and fluids that nourish the Lungs; when it is weak, the Lungs starve. The Kidneys grasp the Qi and send moisture upward - if they are depleted, the Lungs dry out. Even the Liver can contribute when its Yin is deficient, allowing internal heat to rise and scorch the lung tissue. This is why TCM asks not just about your cough, but about your digestion, your energy, your temperature sensations, and your lower back - to trace the true source of the lung's decline.
The quality of your sputum is a critical clue. Dry, sticky phlegm that is hard to cough up points to Lung Yin Deficiency: the lungs lack moisture and are overheating. Thin, watery, frothy sputum signals Lung Yang Deficiency: the lungs lack warmth to transform fluids, so they accumulate as cold dampness.
Thick yellow phlegm with a heavy chest indicates Phlegm-Heat obstructing the airways. Each of these patterns requires a fundamentally different treatment strategy, which is why TCM does not offer a one-size-fits-all remedy for ILD.
classical_quote: 「肺痿吐涎沫而不咳者，其人不渴，必遗尿，小便数。所以然者，以上虚不能制下故也。此为肺中冷，必眩，多涎唾，甘草干姜汤以温之。」
classical_translation: "In lung atrophy, there is spitting of frothy saliva without cough; the patient is not thirsty, but must have incontinence of urine and frequent urination. This is due to deficiency in the upper burner failing to control the lower. This is cold in the lung; there will be dizziness and much drooling and spitting. Use Gan Cao Gan Jiang Tang to warm it."

tcm_diagnosis:
In TCM, Interstitial Lung Disease is understood as a progressive withering of the lung tissue, called Fei Wei (肺痿, fèi wěi). A practitioner starts by listening to the cough and examining the sputum, because the quality of the phlegm is one of the first clues that points toward a particular pattern.
If the cough is dry and the phlegm is scanty, sticky, or difficult to expectorate, and the person feels thirsty with a dry throat, Lung Yin Deficiency is likely. The tongue will appear red with little or no coating, and the pulse feels thin and rapid. This shows the lung’s nourishing fluids are depleted and empty heat is flaring.
When the sputum is thin, clear, and watery, and the person feels cold, has a pale face, and is easily short of breath, the picture shifts to Lung Yang Deficiency. The tongue is pale and maybe puffy, the pulse is deep and weak. Here the lung lacks the warmth to transform fluids, so they accumulate as thin frothy secretions.
A very different pattern is Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs, where the sputum is yellow, thick, and greasy, and the person may feel a heavy sensation in the chest or limbs. The tongue coating is yellow and greasy, the pulse is rapid and slippery. This is a mixed excess pattern on top of underlying deficiency, with dampness and heat obstructing the lung.
If the main complaints are extreme fatigue, poor appetite, and loose stools, the root problem lies in the Spleen and Stomach. A Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency fails to generate enough Qi and Blood to support the lungs. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is weak and thready.
In advanced or chronic cases, Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency may dominate, bringing dizziness, tinnitus, soreness of the lower back and knees, and a deep, thready pulse. The tongue is red with little coating. This reflects a consumption of the body’s deepest reserves, leaving the lungs without the moisture they need.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry cough with scanty, sticky phlegm", "Dry throat and mouth", "Afternoon tidal fever or feeling of heat", "Night sweats", "Heat in palms, soles, and chest", "Flushed cheeks"]
patterns.worse_with: Dry, hot weather, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Overexertion, Stress and irritability, Smoking or polluted air
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and sleep, Cool, fresh air, Moistening foods (pears, almonds, congee), Drinking plenty of water, Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: In Interstitial Lung Disease, the lungs gradually lose their moisture and nourishment. When Lung Yin becomes deficient, the delicate lung tissues dry out and fail to stay supple, leading to the progressive stiffening and shrinking that defines this condition. The resulting emptiness also allows a low-grade heat to kindle inside, which further consumes fluids and triggers the dry cough, sticky phlegm, and afternoon warmth that are so typical.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, dry, thin body with cracks, little or no coating (mirror tongue). Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid, especially weak at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Yin is like the cooling, moist layer that keeps the lungs supple. Heat, dryness, and overwork consume that moisture, while rest, cool air, and moistening foods replenish it. Smoking and spicy foods directly introduce heat and dryness, which burn through the already scarce Yin, whereas gentle breathing and hydration help preserve the fluids that remain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favor moistening, Yin-nourishing foods such as pear, honey, almond, lily bulb, and white fungus soup. Avoid smoking and dry, polluted air; use a humidifier if the environment is arid. Gentle breathing exercises or qi gong can support lung function without exhausting Yin.

patterns.better_with: Warmth and covering the chest, Warm drinks and soups, Rest and gentle breathing, Ginger tea
patterns.why_this_happens: In Interstitial Lung Disease (肺痿), the lung tissue progressively weakens and atrophies. When Lung Yang is deficient, the warming and transforming functions of the Lungs fail. This means fluids are not properly vaporized and instead accumulate as thin, watery, or frothy white phlegm. The chest and back feel cold because Yang cannot reach the surface, and breathing becomes shallow and labored with even mild exertion. Over time, this cold-phlegm obstruction further depletes Lung Qi, creating a cycle of decline that mirrors the fibrotic changes seen in the condition.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, moist body with teeth marks; thin white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the right cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold depletes the body's Yang energy, which is already weak in this pattern, so warmth and rest help preserve and restore it. Warm foods and drinks support the Spleen and Lung's transforming functions, preventing thin fluids from accumulating. Overexertion and excessive talking consume Qi and Yang, worsening shortness of breath and fatigue, while emotional stress can further weaken the Lung's descending and dispersing function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews with ginger, cinnamon, and garlic. Avoid raw, cold, and iced foods and drinks, which further deplete Yang. Keep the chest and back warm with layers, and practice gentle deep breathing exercises to support Lung Qi. Rest when fatigued and consider moxibustion on the upper back to warm the Lungs.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Phlegm and Heat combine in the Lungs, they form a sticky obstruction that blocks the normal descent of Lung Qi. This leads to the hallmark cough with thick yellow sputum, chest tightness, and labored breathing. In interstitial lung disease, this excess pattern can superimpose on an already weakened lung, accelerating tissue damage and scarring as the trapped Heat and Phlegm smolder and irritate the delicate lung tissue.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating that may be thicker in the central and front areas; red prickles may appear on the front third. Pulse: slippery and rapid (滑数 huá shuò), strongest at the right cun (inch) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Heat is an excess pattern fueled by hot, damp-producing foods and environmental irritants. Spicy and greasy foods add Heat and Dampness, thickening phlegm and worsening obstruction. Dairy is notoriously phlegm-forming. Cool air, hydrating fluids, and cooling foods like pear help clear Heat and moisten the Lungs, while rest prevents Qi stagnation that can fan the flames of internal Heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, spicy, and dairy-rich foods that generate Phlegm and Heat. Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, radish, mung beans, and water chestnuts. Stay well hydrated with warm water or chrysanthemum tea. Gentle breathing exercises and avoiding smoky or polluted air help protect the lungs.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen and Stomach are the engine that produces Qi and Blood from food. When they become weak, the whole body runs low on energy, and the lungs are among the first to suffer because they need a steady supply of Qi to keep the airways open and the tissue nourished. Over time, this chronic undernourishment leaves the lung tissue thin, weak, and unable to do its job, producing the gradual shortness of breath and fatigue of lung atrophy (肺痿, fèi wěi).
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with tooth marks on the sides and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and forceless, especially empty at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and routine and is easily overwhelmed by cold, damp, and excess. Cold and raw foods dampen its digestive fire, while overthinking knots the Qi, leaving less energy to be sent upward to the lungs. Warm, cooked meals and rest give the Spleen the gentle support it needs to transform food into usable Qi, gradually restoring the lungs' supply line.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, thoroughly cooked foods like congee, soups, and stewed vegetables. Avoid raw salads, iced drinks, dairy, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Eat smaller, more frequent meals and chew slowly. Gentle daily movement like walking or qigong supports Qi circulation without exhausting you.

patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic interstitial lung disease, the body's deepest reserves of Yin-stored in the Kidneys and Liver-become exhausted. The Kidneys can no longer send moisture upward to the Lungs, while Liver Yin deficiency allows internal heat to rise and further dry the lung tissue. This leads to progressive lung atrophy, a dry cough, and breathlessness, accompanied by systemic signs of deep Yin depletion like dizziness, tinnitus, and a sore lower back.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: Fine, rapid, and wiry; the left Chi (Kidney) position is weak or barely palpable.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Liver Yin are the body's deepest reserves; they are easily depleted by overwork, late nights, and emotional stress, which stir up deficiency heat. Cooling, moistening foods and rest help replenish Yin and calm that heat, protecting the Lungs from further drying and atrophy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, Yin-nourishing foods such as pears, black sesame, walnuts, and congee. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods that consume Yin. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork; gentle practices like tai chi or restorative yoga help preserve Yin without straining the Lungs.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse the lung scarring?
faqs.answer: TCM does not claim to erase established fibrosis, but it can significantly improve the surrounding environment. By reducing inflammation, resolving phlegm, and nourishing the lung tissue, herbal formulas and acupuncture often help slow further deterioration and improve breathing capacity. Many patients find their cough becomes less frequent and their stamina improves, even if CT scans show stable scarring.

faqs.question: How quickly will I feel better?
faqs.answer: Improvement in cough and sputum quality is often the first sign, sometimes within 2-4 weeks. More profound changes in energy levels and shortness of breath usually take 3-6 months of consistent treatment. Because ILD is a chronic condition, TCM aims for gradual, sustained improvement rather than overnight cure.

faqs.question: Can I keep taking my conventional medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should not stop them abruptly. TCM can be used alongside anti-fibrotic drugs, corticosteroids, and oxygen therapy. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your pulmonologist about all treatments you are using so they can coordinate care and watch for any interactions.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks that weaken the Spleen and create phlegm. Dairy products, greasy or fried foods, and excessive sweets tend to generate dampness and phlegm, which can worsen coughing and chest congestion. Spicy, heating foods may aggravate Lung Yin Deficiency patterns, so they are best minimized unless your practitioner advises otherwise.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture help with the shortness of breath?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture points on the chest, back, and limbs can help relax the respiratory muscles, reduce the sensation of breathlessness, and strengthen the Lung and Kidney function that supports deep breathing. Many patients report a calmer, easier breath after sessions, and regular treatment can build cumulative benefit.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe if I'm on oxygen?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture is safe for patients using supplemental oxygen, and herbal formulas are adjusted to avoid any ingredients that might stress the lungs. Be sure your acupuncturist knows your oxygen flow rate, and continue using your oxygen as prescribed during treatments.

research.title: An Overview of Herbal Medicines for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
research.description: This review summarized preclinical and clinical evidence for TCM formulas used in IPF, including Buqi Huoxue Tongluo formula and Qizhukangxian granules. It highlighted anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-fibrotic mechanisms, and noted that several herbs like Huangqi, Danshen, and Danggui show promise in slowing disease progression.
